title: Vishnu Sahasranamam Lyrics with Meaning: Verses 33-34
desc: Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 33 to 34 in Sanskrit with a simple English meaning and how to chant them: 'युगादिकृद्युगावर्तो नैकमायो महाशनः'.
alt: Lord Vishnu, Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 33 to 34 with meaning
caption: Vishnu Sahasranamam, verses 33 to 34.
intro: **Vishnu Sahasranamam** is the thousand names of Lord Vishnu, taught by Bhishma to Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata. This post gives **verses 33 to 34** with the Sanskrit text and a plain English meaning, so you can chant with understanding.
takeaways: The verses here open with **युगादिकृद्युगावर्तो नैकमायो महाशनः**.
Read the Sanskrit slowly, then the meaning, then chant once more.
Thursday and Ekadashi are the days most families keep for Vishnu Sahasranamam.
A short daily portion is better than a rushed full reading.

p: Read the lines aloud, one breath for each half of a verse:
**युगादिकृद्युगावर्तो नैकमायो महाशनः । अदृश्योऽव्यक्तरूपश्च सहस्रजिदनन्तजित् ॥** **इष्टोऽविशिष्टः शिष्टेष्टः शिखण्डी नहुषो वृषः । क्रोधहा क्रोधकृत्कर्ता विश्वबाहुर्महीधरः ॥**

He begins the ages and turns their wheel. Of many maya, the one who swallows all, is that God of gods. Unseen and unmanifest, the victor over thousands and over the endless is he. Dear to all, most distinguished, beloved of the good is he. The destroyer of anger, the one who rouses it, the maker, is that God of gods. His arms reach the whole world and he holds up the earth.
Light a lamp, sit facing east and chant these verses once, then read the meaning silently. Many families take two verses a day and finish the full text in a little under two months.
The names do not need a long ritual. What matters is steady practice, a clear pronunciation and a calm mind.

ul: Thursdays, the day of Vishnu and the planet Jupiter.
Early morning after a bath, or in the evening at the lamp.

faq.q: What do Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 33 to 34 mean?
faq.a: He begins the ages and turns their wheel. Of many maya, the one who swallows all, is that God of gods. Unseen and unmanifest, the victor over thousands and over the endless is he. Dear to all, most distinguished, beloved of the good is he. The destroyer of anger, the one who rouses it, the maker, is that God of gods. His arms reach the whole world and he holds up the earth.
**Bhishma** taught it to Yudhishthira on the field of Kurukshetra, as told in the Anushasana Parva of the Mahabharata.

faq.q: Can I chant a few verses a day instead of the whole text?
faq.a: Yes. A small daily portion with the meaning understood is a common and accepted way to learn it.

note: The Sanskrit is the traditional text. The English is our own plain rendering of the meaning.
